newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Overseas investors drawn to UK bonds, pound.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Overseas investors drawn to UK bonds, pound.

text.p: International investors lapped up British government bonds and increased their exposure to the pound on Thursday morning but shares slipped after an early record.
Analysts said financial markets were growing more at ease with the opposition Labour Party, which looks increasingly likely to form the next government.
Government bonds (gilts) ratcheted up half a point in morning trade while the pound broke above the key 2.40 marks level to hit a 20-month high of 2.4018.

"Sterling was already appreciating before this week but the most recent rally has been driven by the bond market, where there has been substantial overseas interest," said Don Smith, international economist at HSBC Markets.
Gilt futures expiring in December stood at 110-14 in midday trade, up 12/32 on the day. The pound slipped from early highs to 2.3990 marks but was up from 2.3933 on Wednesday.
But in stark contrast British shares faded after setting a new high. The FTSE 100 index of leading shares slid below the 4,000 mark which they had broken above for the first time on Wednesday.
In midday trade the index stood at 3,997.5, down 17.5 on the day.

A pledge for "iron discipline" on public spending from Labour's finance spokesman, Gordon Brown, at this week's party conference and the party's perceived enthusiasm for European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) comforted markets.
"The Labour Party is perceived as more Europe-friendly and that has taken some of the risk away from sterling assets," said Philip Shaw, group economist at Union Plc.
Gilts had missed out on a rally by high-yielding European bonds inspired by greater optimism about EMU after a meeting of EU finance ministers in Dublin last month.

Financial markets concluded the process of European monetary union took a significant step forward at the meeting. But gilts, dogged by a government split over EMU membership and the UK's opt-out clause, were left behind.
Analysts said the party conference this week had allowed gilts to join the convergence party.
"The Labour Party conference has helped sterling fight back. Hidden between the lines of its rhetoric was a stronger commitment to EMU than we have from the government," said Smith.
A general election must be held by May 1997. Labour leads the ruling Conservatives by more than 20 points in the opinion polls.

The gilt market rally spilled over into short sterling futures, contracts used to bet on the path of interest rates in the months and years ahead. That market is now no longer looking for a half-point interest rate rise until June next year, after an election.
The pound's rally has helped change expectations on interest rates, now at 5.75 percent, next year.

A Treasury rule of thumb states that a four percent appreciation in the pound is equivalent to a one percentage point rate rise, so sterling's latest gains could serve to put back the day when rates have to go up again.
"The pound has certainly helped change expectations on rates but it is also a result of the convergence-led gilt market rally," said Shaw.
But the Conservative Party conference next week could force the pound, short sterling and gilts to retrace their steps.
The government is keeping its options open on joining EMU in the first wave in 1999 but a significant number of party members want the government to rule out Britain's early entry.

Government ministers traditionally play to the patriotic sympathies of party delegates and the split over EMU could widen as a result. "Certainly the rally will be limited by the prospect of next week's party conference and the prospect of further government disunity," said Shaw.
